title: Opening More Forest Land May Not Fix Loggers' Biggest Problems
summary: President Trump is widely expected to soon open about 44 million acres of the country's last pristine national forests, a move he says will bring timber jobs back to struggling small towns and help prevent wildfires in overgrown land. Last year he signed executive actions to boost timber sales and reverse the 25-year-old Roadless Rule, which has blocked most new logging on undeveloped national forest land since 2001. The formal repeal is expected early next year. But people who make a living in the forests say the problems are much bigger than access to more trees. Sean Smith, chief executive of Starfire Lumber in Cottage Grove, Oregon, says pressing challenges start with the record-high price of diesel fuel, and inflation pushing up steel, sawblades, ball bearings and many other parts. Smith supports the reversal, saying it could eventually give mills a more reliable local supply, and that much of the nearby Willamette National Forest is dangerously overgrown, making it more prone to catastrophic wildfires. But the Forest Service has struggled to get such projects going even on forests that already have roads, facing lawsuits, red tape and too few workers. Second-generation logger Jeff Brink says few people want to wake at 2 a.m. and drive a log truck for about the same pay as working at McDonald's. Timber sales on federal land have dropped by close to 90 percent since the 1990s, the report says, because of tighter environmental laws and cheaper Canadian lumber imports, and about 400 mills across the Northwest have closed since then, costing about 35,000 jobs. Experts project that overturning the Roadless Rule could raise federal timber sales by only five to ten percent. Environmental groups plan to sue, and retired firefighter Timothy Ingalsbee argues that more roads could bring more human-caused wildfires.
why_it_matters: Decisions about forests affect jobs in small towns, the price and supply of wood, and the risk of wildfires, so opening land alone may not settle the argument.

background_read: National forests are large areas of public forest land, and timber is wood cut from trees for building and other uses.
A rule can block most new roads and logging on undeveloped forest land, even when some people want more timber work there.
Loggers, truck drivers, and mills turn trees into wood products, and their work depends on fuel, parts, workers, and buyers as well as on trees.
Overgrown forest land can hold a lot of dry plants and small trees, which can make wildfires harder to control once they start.
